title: [2011] CCJ 11 (AJ) — LACHMIN DHARAMPAUL v LILOWTI RAMGOPAL AND MAHENDRA RAMGOPAL
text:
[2011] CCJ 11 (AJ)
IN THE CARIBBEAN COURT OF JUSTICE
Appellate Jurisdiction
ON APPEAL FROM THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE
CO-OPERATIVE REPUBLIC OF GUYANA
CCJ Application No. AL 5 of 2011
BETWEEN
LACHMIN DHARAMPAUL APPLICANT
AND
LILOWTI RAMGOPAL
MAHENDRA RAMGOPAL RESPONDENTS
Before the Honourables: Mr Justice Rolston Nelson
Mr Justice Saunders
Mr Justice Wit
Mr Justice Hayton
Mr Justice Anderson
Appearances
Mr Roysdale Forde for the Applicant
Mr Mahendra Ramgopal for the Respondents
JUDGMENT
of
Justices Nelson, Saunders, Wit, Hayton and Anderson
Delivered by
The Honourable Mr Justice Adrian Saunders
on the 14thday of July 2011

[1] This was an application for special leave to appeal a decision of the Court of Appeal.
After hearing the parties we decided to adjourn the application sine die and remit to
Justice Bovell-Drakes, or some other High Court Judge, on an inter partes basis, further
hearing of an application to continue an injunction granted ex parte and a counter-
application to discharge that injunction.
[2] The factual background can very briefly be stated in this manner. On 7th January 2011,
the plaintiffs applied ex parte for an injunction to restrain the defendants from engaging
in certain building works. Justice Bovell-Drakes granted the injunction and set a return
date of 13th January. The plaintiff also applied for the injunction granted to be continued
to the date of the hearing and determination of the substantive action. No inter partes
hearing took place on the 13th January. It would appear that there had been no service
on the defendants. The judge therefore ordered that the injunction be continued to the
20th January.
[3] On the 13th January, after the matter was adjourned, the defendants applied ex parte on
affidavit for the discharge of the injunction. Oddly, this application was filed and heard
ex parte, on the 14th January. In the course of that hearing Mr Justice Bovell-Drakes
varied his earlier order of 7th January and, in lieu of discharging the injunction, the
judge adjourned the matter to the 20th January for an inter partes hearing.
[4] This did not satisfy the defendants. They filed, again ex parte, a Notice of Motion
before the Full Court seeking from that court an order setting aside the ex parte
injunction earlier made by the judge. The Full Court sat on this matter on the 21st
January and set aside the injunction.
[5] When they heard of the decision of the Full Court, the plaintiffs were not pleased. They
promptly lodged an appeal to the Court of Appeal to have the order of the Full Court
set aside. The plaintiffs argued that the Full Court had no jurisdiction to hear and
determine the Notice of Motion; that the Notice was in breach of the Rules and of
natural justice and that the decision of the Full Court was erroneous in point of law.

[6] The Court of Appeal has not yet determined this appeal. The appeal is still pending. On
the 2nd February the plaintiffs filed a summons before a single judge of the Court of
Appeal seeking to set aside the order of the Full Court. This summons was referred to
a full Bench of the Court of Appeal which made an interim order on 29th March, 2011
in which it “suspended until the hearing and determination of the Appeal” the order of
the Full Court and reinstated the order of Mr Justice Bovell-Drakes made on the 13th
January.
[7] The defendants were the ones now dissatisfied. They applied to us for special leave to
appeal this interim order of the Court of Appeal. They argued that the Court of Appeal
lacked jurisdiction to embark upon the appeal.
[8] Did the Full Court lack jurisdiction in the circumstances? And did the Court of Appeal
have jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the Full Court’s decision on an ex parte
application? These are important questions of law. Perhaps one day this court will be
required to give its views on them. But not today.
[9] The brief chronology recited above suggests that both sets of parties considered this
matter sufficiently urgent to rush to the court for relief ex parte. Nothing has been said
to indicate that this great urgency is not still present. Secondly, up to this date, the
merits of the decision to grant the injunction have not yet been heard inter partes as
they should have been at the earliest possible time.
[10] In light of these facts, this Court was of the view that the most orderly and fair manner
in which to dispose of this application was to adjourn it sine die (so that we keep
completely open the jurisdictional and other issues raised relating to the hearings and
orders of the Full Court and the Appeal Court respectively) and that we remit the

matter to the trial judge, Bovell-Drakes J (or some other High Court Judge) for an inter
partes hearing on whether the injunction granted on the 7th January (as amended)
should be continued or should be set aside or be replaced by some fresh order.
[11] The defendants were insistent that they would not withdraw their appeal that is current
before the Court of Appeal. That, of course, is their right. The interim order of the Court
of Appeal, however, must be understood in the context of the fact that at the time that
order was made, there had been no inter partes hearing on the merits of the injunction.
That interim order merely sought temporarily to continue the trial judge’s ex parte
order. It must therefore be interpreted as indicating that that order of the judge obtained
ex parte is to stand until the hearing and determination of the appeal or until the trial
judge makes an order inter partes, whichever is sooner. In all the circumstances, we
made no order as to costs.
